person.name: Franckelson Duvelson
person.headline: MCP server developer — I connect AI assistants to real systems
person.summary: I build Model Context Protocol servers that expose APIs, databases and internal tools to AI assistants as typed, tested tools. Before this I spent three years in high-volume technical support and data processing for US healthcare and telecom accounts, so I can run a discovery call and explain a technical tradeoff to someone who isn't an engineer. I also do security research — fuzzing and protocol analysis — which is mostly the habit of asking what a system wrongly trusts.

projects.name: evm-recon-mcp
projects.summary: An MCP server that lets an AI assistant read deployed smart contracts: fetch bytecode, disassemble it, detect invalid jump targets, read storage slots, derive Solidity storage layouts and decode calldata. 14 EVM chains, no API key.
projects.detail: 8 tools, 15 tests, CI on Node 18/20/22, read-only by design. The distinctive feature is static jump-target validation: a PUSH immediately followed by JUMP/JUMPI has a known target, so it can be checked against the JUMPDEST set, and an invalid one means the call halts exceptionally. It also skips PUSH immediate data correctly, so a 0x5b byte inside push data is not misread as a jump destination. Ships with a public post-release review documenting 8 defects I found in my own code and fixed across two follow-up releases.
projects.why_it_matters: Two of those 8 bugs returned confident wrong answers rather than failing loudly, which is the worst failure mode for an analysis tool. A third shipped a wrong version string past 15 passing tests and green CI, and was caught only by driving the published artifact through the real protocol. That is the standard I work to.

projects.name: QUIC and TLS fuzzing harnesses
projects.summary: Authored the first 10 libFuzzer harnesses for two widely deployed network-security libraries that shipped with none — 6 for a QUIC implementation, 4 for a TLS 1.3 implementation.
projects.detail: Coverage included the frame decoder, stream reassembly, a hand-written ring buffer, a buffer-implementation differential, the connection-ID and path-validation state machine, ACK processing, TLS handshake decoders, the record layer under attacker-chosen fragmentation, 18 typed extension decoders and ECH. Roughly 35M and 82M coverage-guided executions.
projects.why_it_matters: It surfaced a genuine remotely-reachable invariant break that I then proved non-exploitable by replaying the reproducer under a production build — and reported as hardening rather than a vulnerability. Knowing when not to file is most of the job.

projects.name: Assert-oracle fuzzing detector
projects.summary: A build technique that restores compiled-out assertions and makes them the fuzzing oracle, catching memory bugs AddressSanitizer is structurally blind to.
projects.detail: Built with -UNDEBUG and -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS. Demonstrated with a measured positive control: an out-of-range std::vector read that stays inside the heap allocation, which ASan passes clean with exit 0 and the detector aborts on.
projects.why_it_matters: On a hardened target the dominant failure mode is a dead oracle, not a missed bug. This makes the detector provable before you trust a negative result.

projects.name: Threshold-ECDSA key recovery
projects.summary: A state-machine defect in an MPC library leading to private-key recovery. Details withheld while the report is open.
projects.detail: Reproducible from upstream in one command using the project's own CI recipe, with the library source unmodified — only test cases appended. Includes a control arm running the project's own bundled assertion. Vendor and mechanism withheld while the report is open.
projects.why_it_matters: Evidence standard: every claim ships with a control arm proving the delta, and observed is labelled separately from inferred.
